summary:
Assam stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel, including in Assam: transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. Elsewhere in the country, a trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender; at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification; and passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Assam appears in national crime records as one data point within a countrywide pattern. Assam accounted for 2 of the 7 cases registered under the Transgender Persons Act nationally in 2021 and none in the 2023 tally. The source cautions that national counts are tiny — 20 cases across 2019–23 — because of police-registration bias, and reports 2025 survey prevalence of 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence against trans people nationally. Registered cases therefore prove the complaint system is reachable, not that violence is uncommon.

State protective machinery was thin. In the December 2021 national government reply listing the 12 states and union territories that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules, Assam is not among them, so no state welfare body stood in place as of that date. No Assam-specific protective or restrictive statute, ordinance or checkpoint operation is documented in the audited sources.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: national recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026 — including custody treatment of trans people by the Railway Protection Force in Assam — set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 Supreme Court decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and the constitutional reading of sex to include gender identity give a visitor a discrimination-law footing that the criminal code no longer provides in the same form. This sits awkwardly beside the 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which removed gender-identity-specific offences.

External assessment diverges somewhat from community reporting. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 characterises police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and non-systemic, likelier in conservative rural areas, while trans communities report fear of increased sexual assaults under the new code and describe checkpoint encounters as degrading.

Judicial intervention is the recurring counterweight. The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police extended beyond that case to police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, and the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026 against a medical-examination requirement imposed by passport authorities.

The March 2026 amendment narrows recognition to hijra, kinner and intersex applicants, which changes what documents and welfare schemes a self-identifying trans visitor or resident can access, whatever their conduct is otherwise lawful.
localsOnly:
Assam's 2021 and 2023 crime tallies show that complaints under the Transgender Persons Act can be registered there: 2 of the 7 cases recorded nationally in 2021, none in 2023. Against 20 cases nationally across 2019–23, and 2025 survey prevalence of 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence, the gap between reported cases and measured experience is wide and attributed to police-registration bias.

As of the December 2021 national government reply, Assam was not among the 12 states and union territories that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules. Residents therefore had no state welfare body to apply to at that date, and the audited sources do not document one being established later.

Residents reporting violence depend on the national complaint route and on the high courts, which have issued the substantive protective directions on record. No Assam-specific state statute, ordinance or welfare scheme is documented in the audited sources.

Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam described degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024, indicating that police and railway custody is a known site of mistreatment for residents as well as visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Assam constituted a Transgender Welfare Board after December 2021 is not sourced either way; the audited material establishes only its absence as of that date.

Unresolved: whether the March 2026 amendment's implementing rules, and any recognition-document procedure arising from them, have been notified or applied by Assam authorities. No source in the inventory addresses state-level implementation.

Unresolved: whether Assam has issued any state-specific statute, ordinance, directive order or checkpoint operation affecting trans people. The audited sources record none, which is an absence of documentation rather than a positive finding of no such measure.

The 2025 prevalence figures (27.2% physical, 22.3% sexual violence) are national, not Assam-specific; no Assam breakdown is available in the inventory, so they describe the country-level risk environment a visitor enters rather than state-level rates.
